summary:
Last Known Position is an interactive educational platform that explores the stories and known locations of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it transforms mission records and planetary imagery into accessible, evidence-based experiences.

The platform helps users discover abandoned landers, rovers, and other space hardware while understanding how confidently each object's location is known. Its Proof Meter distinguishes between photographed, pinned, estimated, and missing evidence, helping users understand the difference between confirmed observations and uncertain information.

Through AI-assisted storytelling, source-linked explanations, interactive 3D exploration, and Detective Mode, users can investigate the history and physical traces of these machines. The project makes space exploration more engaging while encouraging scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and responsible interpretation of evidence.
details:
How It Works

Last Known Position presents a curated catalogue of abandoned or inactive human-made equipment on the Moon and Mars. Each artifact has an information profile containing its mission history, available location information, supporting imagery, and references to its sources.

The platform uses a project-designed Proof Meter with four evidence labels:

  • Photographed: The artifact is visible in supporting imagery.
  • Pinned: A specific location is recorded.
  • Estimated: The location is approximate or inferred.
  • Missing: A reliable location has not been established in the available sources.

These labels are our own way of communicating evidence confidence; they are not official NASA classifications.

Key Features

  • AI-assisted storytelling: Makes mission and artifact information easier to understand, with source references to support factual claims.
  • Artifact catalogue: Helps users explore selected abandoned or inactive Moon and Mars equipment.
  • Interactive 3D exploration: A stylized rover model lets users explore its major components and understand their functions. It is an educational visualization, not an engineering replica.
  • Detective Mode: Encourages users to examine authentic planetary imagery and investigate visible evidence rather than simply accepting a location claim.

Innovation and Impact

The project's central idea is evidence-first space storytelling. Instead of presenting every location as equally certain, it communicates what is photographed, recorded, estimated, or still unknown. This encourages curiosity, source-checking, and critical thinking among students and space enthusiasts.

Development and Responsible Design

The project combines web-based interactive experiences, 3D visualization, curated mission information, and AI-assisted content. NASA imagery and mission resources are attributed through the project’s references. We aim to distinguish verified information from estimates and avoid presenting uncertain locations as confirmed facts. AI assistance is used to improve accessibility and storytelling, not to replace original mission records or scientific evidence.
